hints: Think about the skin's job. It loses cells every day, so what kind of supply does it need: a one-time batch or a continuous, renewable supply?
Recall the two-part definition of a tissue stem cell: it must keep making copies of itself by mitosis AND produce some daughter cells that go on to specialise.
walkthrough:
**Spot the real problem in skin**

Skin cells are constantly worn away and shed. To replace them for a whole lifetime, you need a permanent source, not just a few cells made once.

Think: continuous replacement needs continuous production.

**Recall what makes a stem cell special**

A tissue stem cell does two things together. It divides by mitosis to self-renew, so the stem cell pool never runs out. At the same time, some of the daughter cells differentiate into specialised skin cells.

This is the key idea: self-renewal + differentiation.

**Pick the feature that enables replacement**

Option C describes exactly that complete mechanism. It explains both the ongoing division and the supply of cells able to become skin cells, so the tissue can be repaired again and again.

options.A: Being undifferentiated and present at birth is true of stem cells, but it does not explain how they keep replacing skin cells throughout life.
options.B: Differentiation alone is only half the story. If all stem cells differentiated with no mitosis to renew them, the supply would quickly run out.
options.C: Correct. Mitosis provides self-renewal to maintain the stem cell population, while some daughter cells differentiate to replace lost skin cells.
options.D: Having the full diploid number of chromosomes is true for most body cells, not a special feature that allows stem cells to replace tissue.
